why_go: Pre-monsoon heat empties the temple crowds; those willing to visit in June get the Nataraja sanctum almost to themselves, with shorter queues at the main corridors and room rates noticeably below the festival-season peaks.

why_not: July is warm and sticky on the Tamil Nadu plains, which makes long circuits of the Nataraja temple complex tiring. Despite the humidity this is not the region's rainy season — those rains arrive with the northeast monsoon in October–December — and July sits well outside the cooler November–February darshan window.

September sits at the transition into Tamil Nadu's northeast monsoon; showers grow more frequent and the town's low-lying streets can waterlog, making the temple circuit uncomfortable and some entry points muddier than usual.

why_go: Summer heat keeps most domestic tourists away from Kanchipuram, so June offers the rare chance to walk the Ekambareswarar and Kamakshi corridors without the usual press of pilgrims; silk weavers are also easier to visit without the festival-season rush.

why_not: July is hot and humid in Kanchipuram, tiring for the long walks between the town's many temples. Inland Tamil Nadu stays largely dry now — its real rains come with the northeast monsoon in October–December — so July offers neither the comfort nor the festival energy of the cooler season that follows.

why_go: June marks the start of the monsoon on the Palani hills, but Kodaikanal's altitude keeps it far cooler than the scorching Tamil Nadu plains; those who can handle mist and short afternoon showers find near-empty trails, low guesthouse rates and a green, quiet lake.

Kotagiri sits on the drier eastern slope of the Nilgiris and stays noticeably cooler than the plains through June; the village is at its greenest, tea gardens look fresh, and the smaller tourist footprint means you'll find budget rooms that are packed solid in April.

Kumbakonam's dozens of temple tanks and corridors are at their least crowded in June; heat drives away the bulk of pilgrims, and those who visit get unhurried access to the Mahamaham tank complex and the main agamas with minimal queuing.

April is one of the last dry windows before the southwest monsoon; Meghamalai's tea estates are in active plucking season, wildlife moves to lower forest elevations, and the access road stays clear without the landslip risk that mid-monsoon brings.

May brings building heat to the Tamil Nadu plains, making Meghamalai's forested ridges a worthwhile retreat; the tea estates are at full flush before the heavy rains, and while pre-monsoon showers begin, the trails and estate bungalow roads are still passable.

August falls mid-monsoon and some jeep zones are restricted, but elephant sightings remain reliable as the larger herds stay in Mudumalai's open grasslands; the forest is dense and green, and fewer safari vehicles on the road improve actual wildlife encounter quality.

June marks the monsoon's arrival on the Nilgiris, bringing mist, rain and leech activity on higher trails, but the temperature stays far below the plains; those prepared for wet weather find quieter cottages, empty rose gardens and the Botanical Garden without weekend crowds.

why_not: April heat on the Deccan foothills makes the 700-step climb to the hilltop shrine punishing; pilgrims face a long exposed ascent under intense sun, and the temple complex at the top offers little shade, making the visit genuinely uncomfortable outside early-morning hours.

June combines peak pre-monsoon heat on the Tamil Nadu plains with the onset of the southwest monsoon; the uncovered 700-step staircase becomes dangerously slippery in rain, the winch queue is long even in the wet, and the heat and humidity make the surrounding town an unpleasant base.

July keeps the monsoon wet spells and heavy humidity of the Tamil Nadu plains; the exposed hillside staircase is slippery after rain, and the combination of intermittent downpours and severe heat makes the steep climb genuinely hazardous for most visitors.

August is still within the southwest monsoon period; showers keep the hillside steps slick, humidity on the plains approach is draining, and the temple complex at the summit is often shrouded in low cloud that obscures the hilltop setting entirely.
